name: Plain Language Summaries for Families
title: Plain Language Summaries for Families
answer: A plain language summary turns key parts of an IEP into a short explanation families can understand, using an approved tool with names removed. It matters because IEP documents are long and technical, and parents may leave meetings unsure what was decided for their child. The summary is a bridge to understanding, not a replacement for the IEP or the family's rights.

sections.body: IEP documents are lengthy, technical, and filled with jargon, so many parents finish meetings without a clear picture of what was decided or what it means for their child. A plain language summary addresses that gap by giving families a short, readable explanation of the main points. It can cover the child's goals, the services they will receive, the supports in class, and whom to call with questions. The summary is meant to help parents understand the plan, not to serve as the official document. It is a bridge to understanding, and teachers should say that clearly when they share one.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give grade bands, so the practice is described generally. A teacher can use an approved tool, with names removed, to turn key parts of the IEP into a short explanation. The summary should include the child's goals, services, classroom supports, and a contact for questions. It can be translated into the family's language and sent through TalkingPoints. The teacher checks every summary against the actual IEP, and a fluent person reviews any translation before it goes to the family.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research. The guidance is presented as a practical way to help families understand IEP decisions, not as a claim supported by a named study. No research citation is offered in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A summary does not replace the IEP or the family's rights to it. Parents are entitled to the full document and to explanations from the team. An error in a summary could mislead a family about their child's rights and services, so the teacher checks every summary against the actual IEP. A fluent person should review translations of anything this important. The decisions about the IEP and the family's rights stay with the team and the official process, while the summary remains only a bridge to understanding.
